characterList.description: The voice of the narrator. Not visually present in the video.
characterList.name: Dr. William J. Doria

content_metadata.description: An educational video by Dr. William J. Doria discussing the principles of spectroscopy, including absorption and emission spectroscopy, the interaction of light with matter, and the equipment used in spectroscopic techniques.

qAndA.question: What are the two most common types of monochromators?
What color does a solution appear to be if it strongly absorbs yellow light?

qAndA.answer: In one design, the monochromator and slit are placed before the sample, while in the other, they are placed after the sample.
qAndA.question: What is the main difference between the two absorption spectrometer designs presented in the video?

qAndA.answer: By heating the sample using a heating coil.
qAndA.question: What is one common way to excite electrons in a sample for emission spectroscopy?
What are two examples of phenomena that can occur while electrons are in an excited state?

activities.description: Narrator introduces the topic (spectroscopy) and addresses the viewers, assuming they've had a recent exam.

mood.description: Neutral - Curious. The upbeat music creates a sense of curiosity for the upcoming topic despite the neutral context of an exam.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction to the topic of spectroscopy.

scenes.thematicElements: The scene sets the stage for the discussion of spectroscopy, framing it as a new topic following an exam.
scenes.title: Introduction

videoEditingDetails.description: Black screen with text: "Physical Chemistry II," "Video Lecture 31," and "Dr. William J. Doria" in green, blue, and red, respectively.
Transition to a video of college students taking an exam, with upbeat background music.

activities.description: Narrator defines spectroscopy and its purpose.
Narrator explains photon absorption and energy transfer in molecules, mentioning possible outcomes like electronic excitation, vibration, and rotation.

mood.description: Neutral - Pensive. The narrator's calm voice and the use of diagrams and visualizations encourage a thoughtful understanding of the information.

narrativeProgression.description: Explanation of the basic principles of spectroscopy, focusing on photon absorption and its effects on molecules.

props.name: Textual definition of "Spectroscopy" appears on a plain grey background.
Simple energy level diagram with a yellow ball representing an electron transitioning to higher levels.
Two rotating 3D models of molecules appear alongside the energy diagram.

scenes.thematicElements: Energy transfer, quantized energy levels, molecular motion.
scenes.title: Basic Principles of Spectroscopy

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition to a plain grey background with text.
Energy level diagram appears.
3D molecule models appear.

activities.description: Narrator discusses challenges in visualizing photon-matter interactions, emphasizing the wave nature of light and electromagnetic fields.
Explanation of light waves as oscillating electric and magnetic fields, and how these fields interact with those of molecules.
Focus shifts to electrical interactions, mentioning magnetic interactions will be discussed later in the course.

mood.description: Neutral - Curious/Confused. The narrator highlights the complexity of visualizing light-matter interactions, creating a sense of curiosity and a potential for confusion if the concepts are not fully grasped.

narrativeProgression.description: Deeper exploration of photon-matter interactions, moving beyond the simple particle model of light to emphasize its wave nature and electromagnetic properties.

props.name: 3D molecule models and energy level diagram remain visible.
A rotating brown amorphous shape representing a photon appears, followed by a red sine wave moving beneath it.
A second sine wave, grey in color and perpendicular to the first one, appears, creating a more realistic visualization of an electromagnetic wave.
A black-and-white diagram of a molecule surrounded by curved lines representing its electric field.

scenes.thematicElements: Wave-particle duality of light, electromagnetic fields, molecular electric fields.
scenes.title: Photon-Matter Interactions

videoEditingDetails.description: A brown amorphous shape appears.
A red sine wave appears.
A grey sine wave appears, perpendicular to the red wave.
Transition to a diagram showing the electric field of a molecule.

activities.description: Narrator explains that the focus will be on electrical interactions for the next several videos, referencing different types of spectroscopy (UV-Vis, IR, and Rotational).
Explanation of the importance of electron's angular momentum in spectroscopy, outlining two types: orbital and spin angular momentum.

mood.description: Neutral - Curious/Pensive. The scene provides specific information about angular momentum, prompting curiosity about its role in spectroscopy.

narrativeProgression.description: Transitioning from general principles to the specific property of angular momentum, setting the stage for future discussions about its importance in spectroscopic techniques.

props.name: Three graphs representing different types of spectroscopy spectra appear: a UV-Vis spectrum, an IR spectrum, and a rotational spectrum.
The graphs disappear, and a textual list of the two types of electron angular momentum appears.

scenes.thematicElements: Types of spectroscopy, angular momentum, electron properties.
scenes.title: Focus on Electrical Interactions

videoEditingDetails.description: Three graphs appear representing different types of spectroscopy.
Transition to plain text listing the two types of angular momentum.

activities.description: Narrator explains that photons also have momentum and spin, leading to the transfer of photon momentum to electrons in the molecule during absorption, resulting in an increase in the electron's energy level. The opposite process (emission) is also mentioned, where electron's energy level decreases by emitting a photon.

mood.description: Neutral - Pensive. The narrator continues to build upon the concepts of energy transfer and momentum, encouraging a thoughtful understanding of the interplay between photons and electrons.

narrativeProgression.description: Further explanation of photon-matter interactions, focusing on the conservation of momentum and how it relates to changes in electron energy levels during absorption and emission.

props.name: Textual list of the two types of electron angular momentum remains on the screen.

The black and white diagram of a molecule with its electric field reappears. The sine wave representing a photon's electromagnetic wave reappears. The energy level diagram with the yellow ball reappears.

The yellow ball moves up, showing the photon being absorbed by the electron and the energy level of the electron increasing. The yellow ball then moves down, showing a photon being emitted and the energy level of the electron decreasing.

scenes.thematicElements: Momentum transfer, conservation of energy, electron excitation and relaxation.
scenes.title: Photons and Momentum

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition back to the black and white diagram of the molecule's electric field and the sine wave representing the photon's electromagnetic wave.
The energy level diagram with the yellow ball reappears.

activities.description: Narrator reiterates the question of how photons transfer momentum to molecules and transitions to explaining the process of detecting interactions between photons and molecules.
Introduction of absorption spectroscopy and its general process, involving a polychromatic light source, monochromator, and detector.
Explanation of monochromators, specifically prisms and diffraction gratings, and how they separate polychromatic light.
Discussion of complementary colors and the color wheel, highlighting the relationship between absorbed and transmitted wavelengths, and how this determines the apparent color of a solution.

mood.description: Neutral - Curious. The narrator provides a detailed explanation of the components and principles behind absorption spectroscopy, piquing the viewer's interest in the subject.

narrativeProgression.description: Transition to discussing the practical aspects of spectroscopy, focusing on the techniques and equipment used to study absorption phenomena.

props.name: The energy level diagram with the yellow ball remains on the screen.

A diagram of a lightbulb, representing a polychromatic light source, appears. A triangle representing a monochromator is added to the right of the lightbulb, followed by a yellow rectangle for the sample and a starburst for the detector. A prism replaces the triangle. A diffraction grating replaces the prism.
A triangular prism with light passing through it and separating into a rainbow of colors appears.
Several diffraction gratings appear, displaying iridescent colors. A person holds a CD and DVD to show the iridescent colors caused by diffraction gratings.

The diagrams disappear, replaced by a color wheel. A yellow section and a blue section on the color wheel are circled, illustrating complementary colors. A circle divided into six sections is then drawn and labeled with the colors of the ROYGBIV acronym, excluding indigo.

scenes.thematicElements: Absorption spectroscopy, monochromators, light diffraction, color theory, complementary colors.
scenes.title: Absorption Spectroscopy

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition to a plain grey background with the title "Absorption Spectroscopy" in pink.
A diagram of a lightbulb is introduced.
A prism replaces the triangle representing the monochromator in the diagram.
Transition to a photo of a prism diffracting light.
Transition to photos of diffraction gratings and a video of someone holding a CD and DVD to show diffraction.
Transition to a color wheel.
Transition back to the diagram of the absorption spectrometer.

activities.description: Narrator emphasizes that the color of a solution is determined by the wavelengths it transmits, not the wavelengths it absorbs.
Continuation of the discussion of complementary colors using the color wheel, providing an example of a solution appearing blue if it strongly absorbs yellow wavelengths.

Introduction of an alternate spectrometer design, where the monochromator and slit are placed after the sample. The narrator explains the benefits of this design, which are not explicitly shown in the video, and mentions the Spec 20 instrument as an example.

mood.description: Neutral - Pensive. The narrator continues to provide factual information and encourages viewers to think critically about the relationship between absorbed wavelengths and the apparent color of a solution.

narrativeProgression.description: Deeper exploration of absorption spectroscopy, focusing on the concept of complementary colors and the practical implications of different spectrometer designs.

props.name: The absorption spectrometer diagram reappears.
The color wheel remains on screen.
The absorption spectrometer diagram is duplicated to show the alternate design with the monochromator after the sample. A photograph of a Spec 20 spectrophotometer appears.

scenes.thematicElements: Color theory, transmitted vs. absorbed wavelengths, spectrometer design, Spec 20 instrument.
scenes.title: Complementary Colors and Spectrometer Design

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition back to the absorption spectrometer diagram.
Transition back to the color wheel.
Transition to a diagram showing the alternate absorption spectrometer design.
A photograph of a Spec 20 spectrophotometer appears.

activities.description: Narrator transitions from absorption spectroscopy to emission spectroscopy, briefly reviewing the concept of emission and its dependence on electron transitions from higher to lower energy states.

Explanation of emission spectrometer design, featuring a sample chamber with a heating coil to excite electrons and a monochromator/slit system placed after the sample to isolate and detect specific emitted wavelengths.
Narrator concludes the video, referencing phenomena like phosphorescence and fluorescence that will be explored in the next video.

mood.description: Neutral - Curious/Excited. The narrator introduces the concept of emission spectroscopy and sets up anticipation for the next video, which will cover exciting phenomena like fluorescence and phosphorescence.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction of emission spectroscopy as another important type of interaction between light and matter.

props.name: The photograph of a Spec 20 spectrophotometer remains on screen. Then the energy level diagram with the yellow ball reappears.

Transition to a diagram of an emission spectrometer with a sample chamber containing a yellow heating coil. Light emits from the sample chamber. A triangle representing the monochromator and a slit are added to the diagram.
The diagram disappears, and three stick figures wearing neon glow stick outfits appear in a dark room.

scenes.thematicElements: Emission spectroscopy, electron excitation, emitted light, fluorescence, phosphorescence.
scenes.title: Emission Spectroscopy

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition to the energy level diagram.
Transition to a diagram of an emission spectrometer.
Transition to a video of stick figures with neon glow stick outfits.

climax.description: Climax not applicable as the content is educational, focusing on explaining the principles and types of spectroscopy.

storylines.description: The video systematically covers different aspects of spectroscopy.

content_metadata.title: Physical Chemistry II: Spectroscopy (1)

trimmingSuggestions.description: The initial black screen with text could be shortened or removed to jump directly into the video of students taking an exam, increasing initial dynamism.
The transition to the Spec 20 photograph (8:58) could be removed, as it does not add significant value to the audio content and interrupts the flow of the video.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, and welcome back to my series of videos for physical chemistry too. By now, you've
had another exam in your class. I hope it went well for you.
Today, I want to tell you a bit more about spectroscopy. As you might remember, spectroscopy
is the study of how light and matter interact, and the ways we can use those interactions
to learn about these structures and properties of molecules. As we'll see, spectroscopy
involves both the absorption and emission of light, and both of these are useful when
we want to study molecules in their properties. As I mentioned earlier, spectroscopy is the
study of how light and matter interact. When a molecule absorbs a photon, the energy
of the photon is transformed into kinetic and potential energy in the molecule. When
the energy of the molecule increases, there are a few different things that could happen.
First, one or more electrons in the molecule could move into a higher energy level. Also,
the molecule could vibrate or rotate more quickly. It can be difficult to visualize how
a photon could be transformed into those types of energy. The reason we might have trouble
picturing this is because we usually fall into the habit of thinking of a photon as a
particle, and this is actually a poor model if we want to understand how photons interact
with matter. It's better to think of it as a wave, but even that can be misleading unless
we keep in mind exactly what light waves are like.
Remember, a light wave is an electromagnetic wave. That means it's made of both an oscillating
electric field and an oscillating magnetic field. If we try to picture a light wave like
an ordinary sine wave, we're actually only drawing one of those oscillating fields. The
other field oscillates at a right angle to the first one, so a picture like this would
be a bit more realistic. So, that's what the electric and magnetic fields of a photon
are like. And as you can imagine, a molecule also has an electric and a magnetic field
thanks to the electrons and protons in the molecule. When a photon and a molecule meet,
it's their electric and magnetic fields that are actually interacting. For now, we're
just going to talk about the electrical interactions. The magnetic interactions are important
too, but we'll worry about those when we talk about NMR spectroscopy later on in the
course. When we talk about UV vis spectroscopy, IR spectroscopy, or rotational spectroscopy,
it's the electrical interactions that we're observing, and that's what we'll talk about
for the next several videos. For most types of spectroscopy, we'll talk about the photons
that are interacting with the electrons rather than the nuclei. That means it's the properties
of the electrons that we need to worry about. As it turns out, the angular momentum of the
electron is particularly important in spectroscopy, so here's an important thing to remember. Electrons
have different types of angular momentum. There's orbital angular momentum, which we get
the symbol of a script letter L, and there's spin angular momentum, which has the symbol
S. It turns out that, just like electrons, photons also have a momentum and a spin. So
when a photon and a molecule interact, the photons momentum is transferred to the electrons
in the molecule. Since momentum and energy are related, absorbing a photons momentum
results in an increase in the electrons energy, which means that the electrons energy level
increases. Of course, an electrons energy level can also decrease if it emits a photon.
So how can a photon transfer momentum to a molecule? To answer that question, it'll
first be helpful to look at how we detect interactions between photons and molecules.
We'll look at the absorption of photons first. In general, here's how we do it. We start
with a polychromatic light source. In other words, a light source that emits a range of different
wavelengths. We shine this light on a sample, but in many spectrometers, we don't hit the
sample with all the wavelengths at once. Instead, we only want a small range of wavelengths
to hit the sample. How do we accomplish that? Well, the first thing we do is place a monocrometer
in the beam of light coming from the source. A monocrometer is a device that separates
polychromatic light into its component wavelengths. The two most common types of monocrometer are
prisms and diffraction greetings. You're probably already familiar with prisms. A prism
is a piece of glass or plastic, usually in the shape of a triangle. The incoming light
is refracted by the glass, and the angle of refraction depends on the wavelength of the
light. As a result, the different wavelengths of light emerge from the prism in different
directions. The other type of monocrometer is a diffraction greeting. A diffraction greeting
is made of a reflective material that's been manufactured so that its surface has a
series of closely spaced parallel ridges. Like a prism, a diffraction greeting can separate
polychromatic light into its component wavelengths. If you've ever seen light reflecting from
the surface of a CD or DVD, you're probably noticed that the light is separated into
a rainbow of colors. That's because the surface of the DVD has a series of ridges similar
to those on a diffraction greeting. Anyway, after passing through the monocrometer, the
light in a spectrometer is separated into its component wavelengths. We can now select
a wavelength of our choice by placing a card with a slit in it in the path of the light.
We position the slit so that the wavelengths were interested in can pass through it and
reach the sample, while the rest of the light is blocked. The light now passes through
the sample and then reaches a detector, which can report the intensity of the light that
made it through the sample, either as the prism transmittance or the absorbance, both
of which we discussed in great detail in video 9. If we want to select a different wavelength,
we just turn a knob on the spectrometer, which causes the prism or diffraction greeting
to rotate so that a different part of the spectrum falls on the slit. If we repeat that
adjustment for many different wavelengths, we can put all the absorbance or transmittance
stated together to generate a spectrum. One thing that's important to realize is that
if a solution absorbs a particular wavelength, that's not the color that the solution appears
to be. Instead, the color of the solution is determined by the wavelengths that are
transmitted through the solution. A rough idea of the color is given by the color wheel,
which you may have seen before if you've taken a class in art, especially painting or
design. The colors on opposite sides of the color wheel are called complementary colors.
In general, if a solution strongly absorbs a particular color, the apparent color of
the solution is the complementary color. So, for example, if the solution absorbs yellow
wavelengths, the solution will appear to be a deep blue. It's not really necessary to
memorize this wheel. You can create a rough version of it by drawing a circle and dividing
it into six sections. These sections can be labeled red, orange, yellow, green, blue,
and violet, similar to the Roy G. Bibv acronym you may be familiar with, but without the
eye for indigo. Let's look at the general setup of a spectrometer again. Although this
is a common spectrometer design, many spectrometers use a slightly different design. In this alternate
arrangement, we don't place the monochrometer and slip before the sample. Instead, we allow
all the light from the polychrometic light source to hit the sample. We then use the monochrometer
and slip to select one of the wavelengths that the sample allows through. This light is
then sent along to the detector. The benefit of this second design is that more light initially
hits the sample, which might cause a photochemical response in the sample that might not occur
with a lower intensity of light that we get with the first design. The second design is
the one used in a spec 20, which is an instrument you might have used before in some of your lab
courses. So far, we've been talking about absorption spectroscopy, but as we saw in video
9, another important interaction between molecules and photons is emission. As you might recall,
emission occurs when we have electrons in a higher energy state and they lose energy to
fall into a lower state. The lost energy is emitted as a photon whose wavelength depends
on the difference between the energies of the two states. So, in order for emission to
occur, we first need to raise the electrons to an excited electronic state. One common
way of doing that is to heat the sample. That means we'll need a different design for
our emission spectrometer. In an emission spectrometer, we first have the sample chamber, which
often has a heating coil around it so that we can heat the sample to a high enough temperature
that we can excite electrons in the sample to a higher state. The sample then emits
light as the electrons return to the ground state. Just as we saw in the second absorption
spectrometer design, we can pass the emitted light through a monochrometer and a slit so
that light of only one wavelength will hit the detector. Well, that's enough new material
for now. In the next video, we'll start looking at some interesting and important phenomena
that can happen while the electrons are in an excited state, including things like phosphorescence
and fluorescence. I hope you'll join me for that. But until next time, have a good week!

youtube_description: In this video, we'll look at a few of the most common general setups for spectrometers, both absorption and emission.
